anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Concurrent transactions compete for mutually incompatible locks, creating blocking chains or deadlocks that halt forward progress until a waiter is granted the lock or a victim is aborted.
MVCC Version Maintenance Anomaly: Obsolete row versions, undo records, and logically deleted index entries accumulate faster than background cleanup workers can reclaim them, inflating data pages and raising visibility-check overhead.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Downstream replicas cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s write-ahead log fast enough, producing widening log-position gaps and preventing log-segment recycling.

Combined phenomena: The database may show long‐running transactions stuck in lock wait queues, a rapidly growing version store and table size, continuous vacuum/clean-up activity that never catches up, and ever-increasing replication apply lag. Lock bloat lengthens transaction lifetimes, so snapshots remain open, preventing version pruning; the extra row versions and larger tables in turn expand I/O and CPU time per statement, lengthening lock hold times and enlarging blocking chains. Meanwhile, the surging volume of undo and redo generated by repeatedly touching bloated pages produces larger log files that must be shipped to replicas, but the replicas are already behind, so additional log segments accumulate on the primary. As log recycling is held back by both open snapshots and replica retention needs, disk space usage spikes on the primary, and replicas deliver increasingly stale reads, reducing failover readiness.

Causal chain: Heavy lock contention freezes or prolongs transactions, pushing the MVCC horizon backward; this prevents cleaners from deleting dead tuples, causing table and index bloat that slows every subsequent statement and amplifies further lock contention. The extra update and cleanup churn inflates WAL generation, which, together with the long-lived transactions that keep old log segments active, overloads the replication pipeline. Replication lag then feeds back by holding even more log segments on the primary, consuming I/O bandwidth and storage that background cleaners and user transactions must now contend with, thereby reinforcing the original lock and version-maintenance problems and driving the system into a mutually aggravating spiral.

entry.official_definition: Terminates any session that has been idle, but not within an open transaction, for longer than the specified amount of time.
entry.trigger_condition: A session is idle and not inside an open transaction longer than the configured threshold.
entry.workload_impact: The session is terminated; the documentation warns about using this with connection pools or middleware.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
